title: Determination of the temperature vs power dynamic behavior of a cryocooler via two independent methods in time and frequency domain
author: Sosso, Durandetto
materials: 2. The diode voltage response is sent to the digital oscilloscope, where it is sampled, averaged and stored. The oscilloscope is set to dc coupling and high input impedance. Furthermore, oscilloscope time-scale has to be set such that at least one full period of the square wave signal is acquired, as shown in Fig. 2. The visualized diode voltage response should be an alternating sequence of exponential rise and decay profiles.Fig. 2One period of the (100 s duration) step input power (yellow) and diode voltage (red) as visualized with the oscilloscope. Ascending and descending exponential decays are averaged and saved.Fig. 2

The number of averages must be chosen such that noise and cryocooler fluctuations are filtered out. Furthermore, this depends also on the required accuracy: more averages means higher accuracy, but a compromise has to be found. Indeed, an acquisition of 100 averages of one period of a 10 mHz signal would take more than 2 h.

steps.title: Generate square‑wave power step
steps.instruction: Program the AWG to output an adequately slow square‑wave voltage (~10 mHz) with low level VL = 0 V and a high level VH chosen so as not to disturb the cryocooler temperature while maximizing signal‑to‑noise. Amplify the signal with the gain amplifier and connect it to the SMD resistor R. The thermal power change per step is P = (VH – VL)² / R = VH² / R.

substeps.instruction: Pass the signal through the gain amplifier
Apply the amplified voltage to the SMD resistor

steps.title: Acquire diode voltage with oscilloscope
steps.instruction: Connect the diode output to a digital oscilloscope set to DC coupling and high input impedance. Adjust the time‑scale to capture at least one full period of the square wave. Sample, average, and store the waveform. Choose the number of averages to suppress noise and cryocooler fluctuations; e.g., 100 averages of a 10 mHz period require >2 h.

substeps.instruction: Set time‑scale for ≥ one period of the square wave
Sample and average the diode voltage

steps.title: Process voltage to temperature
steps.instruction: Add back the previously subtracted DC offset VDC to each acquired voltage point. Convert the corrected voltage to temperature using the diode’s calibrated voltage‑temperature curve.

steps.title: Separate ascending and descending data
steps.instruction: Divide the temperature‑time data into two sets: ascending portions (VL → VH) and descending portions (VH → VL). Process each set independently.

steps.title: Equalize data points per temperature interval
steps.instruction: Because the oscilloscope samples at constant ΔN/Δt, high‑slope regions contain fewer points per temperature interval. Subdivide the full temperature change ΔT into M equal intervals (example M = 5) and select a subset of points so that each interval contains approximately the same number of samples (matching the smallest interval count). This yields a constant ΔN/ΔT for subsequent fitting.

steps.title: Fit ΔT/P to exponential sum
steps.instruction: For each ascending or descending segment compute ΔT/P and fit it to a sum of exponentials: ΔT/P = Σ_i A_i (1 – e^{‑t/τ_i}). Record amplitudes A_i, time constants τ_i and their uncertainties ε(A_i), ε(τ_i).

steps.title: Compute weighted average of fit parameters
steps.instruction: Combine the parameters from the ascending and descending fits by weighted averaging: A_i,avg = (A_i,asc/ε_{A_i,asc}² + A_i,desc/ε_{A_i,desc}²) / (1/ε_{A_i,asc}² + 1/ε_{A_i,desc}²); τ_i,avg is obtained analogously. The final averaged model is ΔT/P|_avg = Σ_i A_i,avg (1 – e^{‑t/τ_i,avg}).

steps.title: Apply sinusoidal power excitation
steps.instruction: Bias the SMD resistor with a sinusoidally varying voltage V(t) = VH·(1 + sin(2π f t))/2, where VL = 0 V. The instantaneous power is Pt = V(t)² / R = VH² (1 + sin(2π f t))/2R. Vary the frequency f over the desired range.

steps.title: Measure diode response with lock‑in
steps.instruction: Connect the diode output to a lock‑in amplifier referenced to the AWG. Set the lock‑in time constant τ_c such that τ_c ≫ 1/f. Record the rms magnitude and phase of the diode signal relative to the reference. Convert rms voltage to temperature using the diode calibration curve.

steps.title: Alternative oscilloscope measurement
steps.instruction: If a lock‑in amplifier is unavailable, use the digital oscilloscope to sample both diode voltage and input voltage (on a second channel). Compute magnitude from peak‑to‑peak or rms values and convert to temperature via the diode calibration. Determine phase φ = 2π·Δt·f from the time delay Δt between input and diode voltage peaks. This method is slower and less accurate, especially when diode amplitude approaches zero.

steps.title: Repeat across frequency sweep
steps.instruction: Repeat the sinusoidal excitation and measurement for a set of frequencies spanning the range of interest, typically spaced equally on a logarithmic scale.

steps.title: Fit magnitude/phase to rational function
steps.instruction: Plot magnitude and phase versus frequency. Fit the complex response with a rational function of s: f(s) = k·(s – z₁)(s – z₂)…(s – z_m) / (s – p₁)(s – p₂)…(s – p_n). Extract zeros z_i, poles p_i, and coefficient k.

steps.title: Derive transfer function from step response
steps.instruction: Compute the pulse response by differentiating the step response ΔT/P: d(ΔT/P)/dt = Σ_i (A_i/τ_i) e^{‑t/τ_i}. Obtain its Laplace transform, or alternatively multiply the Laplace transform of the step response by s, to yield the system transfer function.

description: The two methods presented here are independent and, according to the type of the measurement and to the experimental conditions [1,2], the user can choose the method that better fits his needs. Otherwise, both can be carried out in order to perform a self-consistency check, as presented in Ref. [4].
